provenance.method: Cross-UK waiting-for-assessment question assembled from current NHS/NHS inform/Welsh programme/HSC evidence and existing ND Oracle needs-led adjustment routes. Waiting is not treated as a clinical recommendation or as a reason to withhold support.

question: What support can I look for while waiting for an autism or ADHD assessment in the UK?
why_it_matters: Assessment waits can be long, but many practical, educational, workplace and healthcare needs exist before a diagnostic decision and should not be treated as suspended until diagnosis.
current_understanding: Waiting for assessment is not the same as having no support route. NHS England autism pathway guidance explicitly describes pre-assessment support based on identified needs, and the NHS child ADHD page says support at home and school should continue while waiting. Across the UK, exact services differ, but existing ND Oracle routes can be inspected for workplace adjustments, healthcare communication/access, education support, task organisation, sensory needs and peer/information support without treating those routes as a substitute for clinical assessment. Some specific schemes have their own eligibility rules, so ND Oracle must not promise access merely because a person is awaiting assessment. If distress or risk becomes urgent, the appropriate urgent health/mental-health route is separate from the routine neurodevelopmental waiting list.
evidence_needed: Nation- and locality-specific pre-assessment support offers and waiting-list contact arrangements for adult and child autism/ADHD pathways.
Clearer four-nation education and workplace evidence on support that does not require diagnosis.
reopening_conditions: National assessment services introduce new pre-assessment support duties or pathways.
Relevant adjustment/support eligibility rules materially change.
dissent: Some services are diagnosis-gated while others are needs-led; ND Oracle should neither imply that diagnosis is always required nor that every support route is diagnosis-free.
